title: Parliament
summary: How Parliament is made up, how it works, makes laws, passes the budget and checks the government.

subcards.title: Composition: Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha
subcards.summary: What Parliament is made of, how each House is formed, and who is stronger.
at_a_glance: Articles 79–83 cover composition; the whole Parliament chapter is Part V, Articles 79–122
The President, the Rajya Sabha and the Lok Sabha
Maximum 250 (238 elected and 12 nominated); at present 245
Maximum 550 (530 from States and 20 from Union Territories); at present 543
Lok Sabha: 5 years. Rajya Sabha member: 6 years; one-third of members retire every second year
25 Lok Sabha seats (4 reserved for SC, 1 for ST); 11 Rajya Sabha seats
Seats per State frozen until the first census after 2026 (84th Amendment, 2001)
106th Amendment came into force on 16 April 2026, but the quota has not started yet (as of Nov 2026)

items: Article 79: "There shall be a Parliament for the Union which shall consist of the President and two Houses" — the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) and the House of the People (Lok Sabha). The Prime Minister, Council of Ministers and Supreme Court are NOT parts of Parliament.
So Parliament has three parts: the President, the Rajya Sabha and the Lok Sabha. Art 79 is the Article that makes Parliament bicameral (bicameral = having two Houses).

President is NOT a member of either House (Art 59) and does not sit in Parliament (except to give an address), yet is an integral part of it, because a bill passed by both Houses cannot become law without the President's assent.

The President's functions linked to Parliament: summons both Houses (calls them to meet) and prorogues them (ends a session); dissolves the Lok Sabha (never the Rajya Sabha); addresses both Houses; issues ordinances when Parliament is not in session.

Model: India follows the British pattern. In Britain the Crown is part of Parliament ('Crown-in-Parliament'); in India the President is part of Parliament ('President-in-Parliament'). India does not follow the American model — the US President is not part of Congress.
Parliament is the national legislature (law-making body) of the Union. Legislative power belongs to Parliament, not to the President, the PM or the Council of Ministers.
Word 'Parliament' comes from French 'parler' = to speak.

Parliament is in Part V, Chapter II, Articles 79–122. Art 80 deals with the composition of the Rajya Sabha; Art 81 with the composition of the Lok Sabha; Art 82 with readjustment of seats after each census; Art 83 with the duration of the Houses; Art 84 with qualifications of members.

blocks.title: Names and key dates
head: Item
Fact
rows: The Hindi names 'Rajya Sabha' and 'Lok Sabha' were adopted in 1954. The Chairman, Dr S. Radhakrishnan, announced the name Rajya Sabha on 23 Aug 1954
Rajya Sabha is also called the Upper House, Second Chamber, House of Elders or Council of States. Lok Sabha is also called the Lower House, First Chamber, Popular House or House of the People
Constituted in 1952, after the 1951–52 general election. Both Houses first sat on 13 May 1952
The Constitution's original maximum for States was 500; 489 seats were filled by direct election in 1952

Inaugurated in May 2023. The Lok Sabha chamber seats 888 and the Rajya Sabha chamber 384; for a joint sitting of both Houses, up to 1,272 can sit. The first bill taken up there was the women's reservation bill (Sept 2023)

blocks.title: Strength (Art 80 + Fourth Schedule)
head: Item
Constitution allows (maximum)
At present
rows: Elected representatives of States and Union Territories (UTs)
Only 3 UTs have seats: Delhi 3, Jammu & Kashmir 4, Puducherry 1 (the other UTs are too small)
blocks.note: The Fourth Schedule (not the Fifth) lists how many Rajya Sabha seats each State and UT gets.

blocks.title: How States are represented
items: Seats are given to States on the basis of population, so States get different numbers: Uttar Pradesh 31 (highest), Maharashtra 19, Tamil Nadu 18, Andhra Pradesh 11, Odisha 10, Telangana 7, Jharkhand 6. Small States like Goa, Sikkim, Tripura, Mizoram and Nagaland get 1 each.
India does NOT give equal seats to States. The US Senate does: 2 seats for every State, 100 in total.

Election: by the ELECTED members of the State Legislative Assembly (MLAs). Nominated MLAs and members of the Legislative Council (MLCs) do not vote. Method: proportional representation by single transferable vote (STV — each voter ranks candidates 1, 2, 3 and so on; extra votes of a winner pass to the next preferences). India borrowed this method from South Africa.
So elected MLAs are the only people who vote in both elections: in Lok Sabha elections as ordinary voters, and in Rajya Sabha elections as MLAs.
UT representatives: elected by an electoral college (a special body of voters) formed for that UT, also by STV.
Quota of votes needed to win = (valid votes ÷ (seats to be filled + 1)) + 1. Example: 4 seats; 180 valid ballots, each valued 100, give 18,000 votes; 18,000 ÷ 5 = 3,600; add 1 = 3,601.

Open ballot (since 2003, by an amendment to the Representation of the People Act): an MLA who belongs to a party must show his marked ballot paper to the party's authorised agent. Purpose: to stop cross-voting (voting against one's own party) and the use of money to buy votes.

Domicile rule removed (2003): a candidate no longer needs to be a voter or resident of the State he is elected from; he must be a voter in ANY parliamentary constituency in India. The Supreme Court upheld both changes (open ballot and no domicile) in the Kuldip Nayar case (2006).
Rajya Sabha is called the 'Council of States' because it represents the States. It keeps the federal balance by protecting the interests of the States.

Rajya Sabha is presided over by the Vice-President, who is its ex-officio Chairman (Chairman because of his office) and is not a member of the House. The Deputy Chairman is elected by the members from among themselves. → see parl-officers

Other indirect elections for contrast: the Vice-President is elected by an electoral college of members of both Houses; in a State Legislative Council some members are elected by graduates and by teachers.

blocks.title: Nominated members (Art 80(3))
head: Point
Fact
rows: Literature, science, art and social service. Sports, eloquence (public speaking) and co-operation are NOT listed
To give eminent persons a seat without having to fight an election. The US Senate has no nominated members
Can become ministers (no constitutional bar). Can vote in the Vice-President's election but NOT in the President's election

Sachin Tendulkar (2012; exam keys put him under 'art', because sports is not a listed field); Ranjan Gogoi (former Chief Justice of India, 2020); Sudha Murty (writer in Kannada and English, nominated March 2024); Harivansh (nominated again in April 2026 and re-elected Deputy Chairman for a 3rd term, as of Nov 2026)

blocks.title: Reform commissions on Rajya Sabha
head: Commission
View
rows: No change needed in Rajya Sabha's role; it did NOT suggest equal seats for States
Its boldest idea: equal number of Rajya Sabha seats for every State

sections.heading: Lok Sabha: composition, seats and reservation

blocks.title: Strength (Art 81)
head: Item
Constitution allows (maximum)
At present (2024 allocation)
rows: 543, all elected (older exam keys say 545, counting the 2 Anglo-Indians)
None now (the President's nomination of 2 Anglo-Indians under Art 331 ended on 25 Jan 2020)
blocks.note: For comparison (Arts 170, 171): a State Legislative Assembly has maximum 500 and minimum 60 members; a Legislative Council has maximum one-third of the Assembly's strength and minimum 40.

blocks.title: Election
items: Members from States are directly elected by the people from territorial constituencies (areas), by universal adult franchise (every adult citizen votes; voting age 18, lowered from 21 by the 61st Amendment, 1988). System: first-past-the-post (the candidate with the most votes wins; one member per constituency).
UT members: Parliament decides how they are chosen. Under the Union Territories (Direct Election to the House of the People) Act, 1965, they too are directly elected.

Two equality rules: (a) the ratio of seats to population is the same for all States (this rule does not apply to a State with population not exceeding 6 million); (b) within a State, every constituency has about the same population.

The Constitution (Arts 81 and 170) gives only the maximum seats and the principles. The actual allocation of seats and election details are in the Representation of the People Acts of 1950 and 1951, made by Parliament.

A Lok Sabha candidate must be a voter in any parliamentary constituency in India (Section 4(d) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951). Minimum age: 25 for Lok Sabha and State Assembly; 30 for Rajya Sabha and State Legislative Council. → see parl-members
After the results, the Election Commission issues the notification that constitutes (formally forms) the new Lok Sabha.
Election disputes (election petitions) about MPs are decided by the High Court, with appeal to the Supreme Court — not by the Election Commission or the Chief Election Commissioner.

blocks.text: Readjustment of seats (delimitation = redrawing the number of seats and constituency boundaries) is to be done after every census (Art 82). Parliament decides which authority does it, through the Delimitation Commission Acts of 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002.

head: Amendment (year)
Change
rows: Changed the composition of the Lok Sabha after the reorganisation of States (raised the number of seats elected from States)
Maximum seats changed: States raised from 500 to 525; UTs reduced from 25 to 20
Maximum seats for States raised from 525 to 530

blocks.title: Status (as of Nov 2026)
items: Census 2027: house-listing phase 1 April–30 September 2026; population count 25 January–28 February 2027 (reference date 1 March 2027). No new delimitation has started.

The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 was defeated in the Lok Sabha on 17 April 2026: 298 voted for and 230 against, short of the two-thirds majority needed. It aimed to raise the Lok Sabha to 850 seats and to redraw seats on the 2011 census, so that the women's quota could start in 2029. The Delimitation Bill 2026 was withdrawn the same day.

blocks.title: Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 — Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam
head: Point
Fact
rows: Introduced as the Constitution (128th Amendment) Bill, 2023; it was the first bill taken up in the new Parliament building
One-third (as nearly as possible) of the seats filled by direct election are reserved for women in the Lok Sabha, the State Assemblies and the Delhi Assembly
One-third of the seats reserved for SCs and STs go to SC and ST women
Rajya Sabha and State Legislative Councils; there is no separate sub-quota for OBC women
15 years from commencement; Parliament may extend it by law
Only after delimitation (redrawing of seats) based on the figures of the first census taken after the Act's commencement (Art 334A)

The Act came into force on 16 April 2026, but the reservation has NOT started yet (it waits for the census and delimitation); it did not apply to the 2024 Lok Sabha election. In July 2026 the Supreme Court issued notice (asked the Centre to reply) on a plea for early implementation

blocks.title: Women in Lok Sabha
items: 15th Lok Sabha (2009): women crossed 10% for the first time (about 59 women).
17th Lok Sabha (2019): 78 women (about 14%) — highest ever.
18th Lok Sabha (2024): 74 women (about 13.6%).
Reserving one-third of seats in legislatures for women needs a constitutional amendment; a party giving one-third of its tickets to women does not.

blocks.title: Duration (Art 83)
head: Aspect
Rajya Sabha
Lok Sabha
rows: Permanent (continuing) House; it is never dissolved
Each member's term is 6 years — fixed by the Representation of the People Act, 1951, NOT by the Constitution
5 years from the date of its first meeting (Art 83(2)); then it is dissolved automatically, without any order
One-third of members retire every second year (staggered terms); members can be re-elected any number of times; the first batch to retire was decided by lottery

The President may dissolve it earlier on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Arts 74, 85) — no Emergency is needed; e.g. when the government loses a confidence vote and no other government can be formed
Only during a National Emergency, by a law of Parliament, for 1 year at a time (any number of times), but not beyond 6 months after the Emergency ends

items: Fifth Lok Sabha (1971–77) was due to end on 18 March 1976. Two Acts of 1976 extended it, first to 18 March 1977 and then to 18 March 1978. It was actually dissolved on 18 January 1977, after 5 years 10 months 6 days.
A State Legislative Council is also a permanent (continuing) House, but it is weaker than its Assembly. Neither the Council nor the Rajya Sabha can be dissolved.

When the Lok Sabha is dissolved, the Speaker stays in office until just before the first meeting of the new Lok Sabha. After a session is prorogued (ended), only the President can summon the House again. → see parl-sessions

sections.heading: Lok Sabha vs Rajya Sabha: full comparison

blocks.title: Lok Sabha vs Rajya Sabha
head: Aspect
Lok Sabha
Rajya Sabha
rows: None (2 Anglo-Indians were nominated until Jan 2020)
Indirect, by elected MLAs, by single transferable vote (proportional representation)
Permanent House; each member serves 6 years
Cannot introduce, amend or reject it; must return it within 14 days, with or without recommendations (Art 109); the Lok Sabha may accept or reject those recommendations
Can discuss the budget (Annual Financial Statement) but cannot vote on demands
Only here, because the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible only to the Lok Sabha (Art 75(3)). The motion need not give reasons; it is not in the Constitution but in the Lok Sabha Rules
Cannot remove the government; can only discuss and criticise it
Only the Lok Sabha can pass a resolution (by simple majority) to end it
The Speaker presides; the Lok Sabha, being larger, usually wins
Weaker because it has fewer members. There is no joint sitting for Money Bills or Constitution Amendment Bills
Equal (there is no joint sitting, so if the Houses disagree, the bill fails)
Equal share in electing and impeaching the President
Takes part in the election; agrees to the removal resolution by simple majority
The removal resolution can start ONLY here and needs an effective majority (a majority of all the then members) (Art 67)
Equal (removal motion can start in either House: signed by 100 Lok Sabha members or 50 Rajya Sabha members)
Ordinances, all three types of Emergency, and reports of the CAG, Finance Commission and UPSC
Equal power to approve or consider
Equal. If the Lok Sabha has been dissolved, a proclamation approved by the Rajya Sabha alone stays in force until 30 days after the new Lok Sabha first sits

Special power: a resolution supported by two-thirds of members present and voting. It is valid for 1 year (can be renewed); the law made under it lapses 6 months after the resolution ends. No Emergency is needed

Special power: a resolution supported by two-thirds of members present and voting; then Parliament creates the service by law (e.g. Indian Forest Service, 1966). Art 312 also allows an All-India Judicial Service
The PM and ministers may be from either House
A PM who is a Rajya Sabha member cannot vote in the Lok Sabha (e.g. on a no-confidence motion)

blocks.text: Verdict: the two Houses do not have equal (co-equal) status. The Rajya Sabha is equal in most matters, except money matters and control over the Council of Ministers. It is weaker than the US Senate but stronger than the British House of Lords. The Rajya Sabha CANNOT authorise State Assemblies to make laws on Union List subjects.
see Legislative procedure (money bill, joint sitting)

items: Parliament is the President and the two Houses (Art 79) — not the PM and not the Council of Ministers.
Rajya Sabha seats are listed in the Fourth Schedule (not the Fifth); they are based on population, not equal for every State as in the US Senate.
A Rajya Sabha member's 6-year term comes from the Representation of the People Act, 1951, not from the Constitution.
Lok Sabha maximum is now 550 (it was 552 only before Jan 2020); the present 543 = 524 from States and 19 from UTs.
104th Amendment (2019): SC/ST seat reservation extended to 2030; Anglo-Indian nomination ended (25 Jan 2020).
Lok Sabha extension during an Emergency: 1 year at a time, and at most 6 months after the Emergency ends (not 1 year).

106th Amendment: in force from 16 April 2026, but the women's quota starts only after delimitation based on the next census; it does not cover the Rajya Sabha or Legislative Councils; it has no OBC sub-quota.
Arts 249 and 312 need two-thirds of Rajya Sabha members present and voting; removal of the Vice-President needs an effective majority (majority of all then members) in the Rajya Sabha.

subcards.summary: Who can become an MP, who loses the seat, and what protection MPs get.
at_a_glance: Art 84 and the Representation of the People Act (RPA), 1951
Art 102 lists the grounds; under Art 103 the President decides, and must follow the Election Commission's opinion
Art 101; the House may declare a seat vacant after 60 days' absence
Art 99 (form in the Third Schedule); Art 104 penalty: ₹500 for each day
Art 105 for Parliament; Art 194 for state legislatures

blocks.title: Qualifications
head: Source
Requirement
rows: Must be a citizen of India

Must make an oath or affirmation (a solemn promise without God's name) before a person authorised by the Election Commission. In it he promises loyalty to the Constitution and to uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India
Age: at least 25 years for Lok Sabha, 30 years for Rajya Sabha
Must have any other qualification that Parliament prescribes by law
Must be registered as a voter (elector) in ANY parliamentary constituency in India. The same rule applies for both Houses
To contest a seat reserved for Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes, he must belong to that group. An SC or ST person may also contest a general (unreserved) seat

blocks.title: Rajya Sabha domicile change
items: Before 2003: a Rajya Sabha candidate had to be a voter (elector) of the state he wanted to represent (this is called the domicile rule).
A 2003 amendment to the RPA 1951 removed this rule. Now a voter registered anywhere in India can be elected to the Rajya Sabha from any state, for example Andhra Pradesh.
Kuldip Nayar case (2006): Supreme Court UPHELD this change (did not strike it down).
The 6-year term of Rajya Sabha members is fixed by RPA 1951, not by the Constitution.

blocks.title: What is NOT required
items: No educational qualification (not literacy, not matriculation, not graduation).
No need to be a voter of the particular constituency you contest. Being a voter in any constituency in India is enough.

blocks.text: Minimum age at a glance: Lok Sabha 25, Legislative Assembly 25, Rajya Sabha 30, Legislative Council 30.

blocks.title: Art 102(1) — disqualifications in the Constitution
head: Ground
Note
rows: Holds an office of profit under Union or state government
A minister's post does not count as an office of profit. Parliament can also exempt other offices by law
Only if a competent court has declared him so
Means a person declared bankrupt by a court who has not yet been released from that status. This ground is in Art 102 itself, not in the RPA
Is not a citizen of India, or has voluntarily taken another country's citizenship, or owes loyalty to a foreign state
Is disqualified by any law made by Parliament
The RPA 1951 grounds (table below) apply through this clause
Art 102(2): defection (leaving or disobeying one's party) under the Tenth Schedule
Decided by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha or the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, not by the President
blocks.note: For state legislators (MLAs and MLCs), the same list is in Art 191.

blocks.title: Art 103: who decides disqualification (all grounds except defection)

steps.step: Question arises whether an MP is disqualified (e.g. office of profit)
President must obtain the Election Commission's opinion
President must act according to that opinion
steps.detail: The opinion is binding, so the President has no choice of his own. His decision is final.

blocks.title: Office of profit
items: The term 'office of profit' (a government post that gives pay or benefits) is NOT defined in the Constitution; courts have explained its meaning.
The Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act, 1959 lists offices of profit whose holders are NOT disqualified from being MPs.
Laxmikanth (and the exam answer key) say this Act has been amended five times.

blocks.title: RPA 1951 — main grounds and duration
head: Section
Ground
Disqualified for
rows: Convicted of a listed serious offence, for example: promoting enmity between groups, bribery, undue influence at elections, offences under the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act 1971, or practising untouchability (Protection of Civil Rights Act)
Any sentence is enough. If only a fine: 6 years from the date of conviction. If jailed: from the date of conviction until 6 years after release
Convicted of a social offence, for example: dowry, adulteration of food or drugs, hoarding, or sati
Only if jailed for at least 6 months. Then: from the date of conviction until 6 years after release
Convicted of any other offence and jailed for 2 years or more
From the date of conviction until 6 years after release
Found guilty of a corrupt practice at an election (for example bribing voters)
Up to 6 years. The President decides the period, on the Election Commission's opinion
Dismissed from government service for corruption or disloyalty to the State
Has a running (subsisting) contract with the government to supply goods or carry out works
As long as the contract lasts
Managing agent, manager or secretary of a company or corporation (not a co-operative society) in which the government holds at least 25% share
As long as he holds that post
Failed to submit the account of election expenses in the time and manner required by law
3 years from the date of the Election Commission's order
blocks.note: Preventive detention (being held in jail to prevent a possible offence, without a conviction) is NOT a disqualification.

blocks.title: Case
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Struck down Section 8(4) of the RPA 1951. That section let sitting MPs and MLAs keep their seat if they appealed within 3 months of conviction

A legislator convicted and jailed for 2 years or more now loses the seat from the date of conviction. The Bill brought to undo this ruling (Representation of the People (Second Amendment and Validation) Bill, 2013) was withdrawn, so the ruling was NOT nullified

blocks.text: For defection grounds and the Tenth Schedule, see Anti-defection law

blocks.title: Art 101 — when an MP vacates the seat
head: Situation
Result
rows: Must tell within 10 days which House he wants to keep. If he does not, his Rajya Sabha seat becomes vacant
Sitting member of one House elected to the other
Seat in the first House becomes vacant
Elected from two seats in the same House
Must keep one seat and resign the other; a bye-election is held for the seat he leaves. If he does not choose, both seats become vacant
Elected to both Parliament and a state legislature
His Parliament seat becomes vacant if he does not resign the state seat within 14 days
Seat becomes vacant immediately under Art 101(3)(a). No ruling or House resolution is needed
Writes to the Speaker (Lok Sabha) or Chairman (Rajya Sabha). The seat is vacant only when the resignation is accepted; it may be refused if it is not voluntary or genuine
Absent from all meetings for 60 days without permission
The House may declare the seat vacant. Periods when the House is prorogued (session ended) or adjourned for more than 4 days are not counted in the 60 days
Seat also becomes vacant if: a court declares his election void; the House expels him; he is elected President or Vice-President; or he is appointed Governor of a state
blocks.note: If a disqualified person gets elected, the High Court can declare the election void under the RPA 1951. An appeal against that order goes to the Supreme Court.

blocks.title: Oath (Art 99) and penalty (Art 104)
items: Before taking his seat, every member takes an oath before the President or a person the President appoints. The words of the oath are in the Third Schedule.
Until he takes the oath, a member cannot vote, take part in the work of the House, or claim parliamentary privileges.
Art 104: a penalty of ₹500 for each day a person sits or votes in the House (a) before taking the oath, or (b) knowing that he is not qualified or is disqualified.

blocks.title: Salary and allowances (Art 106: amounts are fixed by Parliament by law)
head: Item
Amount
rows: Salary, Allowances and Pension of Members of Parliament Act, 1954
Not provided in the Constitution; Parliament provided pension in 1976
₹1,24,000 per month (raised from ₹1 lakh; notified on 21 March 2025, effective from 1 April 2023) (as of Nov 2026)
₹31,000 per month (was ₹25,000), plus ₹2,500 per month for each year of service beyond 5 years (was ₹2,000)

blocks.title: MPLADS (MP Local Area Development Scheme)
items: The MP only recommends works that create lasting community assets (for example drinking water, roads). The district authority checks whether the work is eligible and gets it done.
The Union government pays the full amount. Money not spent in a year does not lapse; it carries over (non-lapsable).
Entitlement: ₹5 crore per MP per year (not ₹10 crore).
A Lok Sabha MP recommends works in his own constituency. An elected Rajya Sabha MP recommends works anywhere in the state that elected him. A nominated MP can recommend works anywhere in India.
Run by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), not the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs.

blocks.title: Odd facts asked in exams
items: Indian Parliamentary Group: formed in 1949. The Lok Sabha Speaker is its president by virtue of his office (ex officio).
Oldest member of 16th Lok Sabha (2014): L.K. Advani.
Lok Sabha's 2022 booklet of unparliamentary words (words not allowed in the House) included 'Shakuni', 'Nautanki' and 'Girgit'. 'Chakkar' was NOT in it.

Parliamentary privileges are special rights and protections given to the Houses, their committees and their members. Without them, Parliament could not work freely or protect its dignity.

blocks.title: Who gets them
items: MPs, and also every person who has a right to speak in a House or its committees, such as the Attorney General and Union ministers (Art 105(4)).
Committees of Parliament also get them (Art 105(3)).
NOT the President, even though he is a part of Parliament.

blocks.title: Collective vs individual privileges
head: Aspect
Collective (House as a whole)
Individual (each member)
rows: The House can: publish its proceedings and stop others from publishing them; hold secret sittings; make rules for its own procedure; punish members AND outsiders for breach of privilege or contempt; get immediate information when a member is arrested; summon witnesses and documents. Courts cannot inquire into its proceedings. No one can be arrested, and no legal process served, inside the House premises without the presiding officer's permission

Freedom of speech in Parliament: no court case can be filed for anything he says or any vote he gives there (Art 105(1) and 105(2)). No arrest in CIVIL cases during a session and for 40 days before and after it. Exempt from jury service. Can refuse to appear as a witness in a court case while Parliament is in session
Freedom of speech must follow the Constitution and the rules of the House. Protection from arrest does not cover criminal cases or preventive detention

blocks.title: Breach of privilege vs contempt of the House
head: Aspect
Breach of privilege
Contempt of the House
rows: Violation of a specific privilege of a member or of the House
Any act that obstructs the House in its work or lowers its dignity
Narrower: every breach of privilege is also a contempt
Wider: a contempt need not be a breach of any specific privilege
Disobeying a lawful order of the House

items.what: Art 105 named two privileges: freedom of speech and the right of publication. All other privileges were to be the same as those of the British House of Commons

44th Amendment: other privileges are those the House had on 20 June 1979 (the date this part came into force). The mention of the British House of Commons was dropped, but this was only a change of words, not of substance
No single law lists all privileges. They come from five sources: the Constitution, laws made by Parliament, rules of the Houses, parliamentary conventions (accepted practices) and court rulings

items: Art 105(3): Parliament may define privileges by ordinary law; Art 194(3) gives the same power to state legislatures.
Such an ordinary law cannot change Art 105 itself. Changing the Article needs a Constitutional amendment under Art 368.

Art 361A (added by the 44th Amendment, 1978): newspapers, radio and TV are protected from court cases when they publish substantially true reports of proceedings. This protection does not cover secret sittings.
Art 105 is for Parliament; Art 194 is the same for state legislatures.

blocks.title: Cases
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Keshav Singh case (Special Reference No. 1 of 1964; opinion given 30 September 1964, reported in 1965)
A clash between the privilege of the Uttar Pradesh Legislative Assembly and the power of the Allahabad High Court
Held that legislative privileges are subject to the Constitution and do not override it

5 judges, 3:2 majority. In the 1993 no-confidence vote, MPs who took bribes and voted as agreed were held immune from prosecution under Art 105(2). Ajit Singh, who took a bribe but did not vote (abstained), was not immune
Gave bribe-taking MPs immunity. Now overruled by Sita Soren (2024)
Upheld the expulsion of MPs in the cash-for-query case (MPs took money to ask questions in Parliament). Parliament has an implied power under Art 105 to expel members
Courts can still examine such decisions for gross illegality or violation of the Constitution, but not for a mere mistake in procedure

7 judges, unanimous, led by Chief Justice D.Y. Chandrachud (4 March 2024). Sita Soren, a JMM MLA from Jharkhand, allegedly took money to vote in the 2012 Rajya Sabha election but voted for her own party's candidate. She claimed immunity under Art 194(2)
Overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao: bribery is NOT protected by Art 105(2) or Art 194(2). The offence is complete when the bribe is accepted, whether or not the vote is cast as promised
blocks.note: Other cases asked in matching questions: S.P. Gupta case (1981) widened locus standi (the right to approach the court) for public interest litigation (PIL). Nabam Rebia case (2016): a Speaker facing a notice for his removal should not decide disqualification petitions.

head: Article
Subject
rows: Powers and privileges of Parliament (Art 105) and of state legislatures (Art 194)
Each House makes rules for its procedure
Courts cannot question proceedings of Parliament on the ground of irregularity of procedure
Same bar on courts for proceedings of the state legislature

blocks.note: Art 122 and Art 212 stop courts only on grounds of mere irregularity of procedure. Courts can still act if there is substantive illegality or a violation of the Constitution.

blocks.title: Attorney General and ministers in Parliament
items: Art 88: the Attorney General (AG) and ministers can speak and take part in either House and in any committee of which they are named members, but cannot vote there.
A minister votes only in the House of which he is a member.
The AG gets all the privileges of an MP (Art 105(4)), including freedom of speech. Art 76 creates the office of AG.
The Solicitor General has no such constitutional right to take part in Parliament. The AG resigning when the government resigns is only a convention (practice), not a rule in the Constitution.
An MP elected Vice-President vacates the parliamentary seat on entering office (Art 66).
Minimum ages: Lok Sabha and Legislative Assembly 25; Rajya Sabha and Legislative Council 30. No educational qualification is required.
'Undischarged insolvent' is a ground in Art 102, not in the RPA.
Art 103: the Election Commission's opinion BINDS the President. Defection is decided by the Speaker or Chairman, not the President.
An MP disqualified under Art 102 loses the seat immediately (Art 101(3)(a)).
Kuldip Nayar (2006) UPHELD the removal of the domicile (home-state) rule for Rajya Sabha.
Lily Thomas (2013) struck down Section 8(4) of the RPA; the Bill to undo it was withdrawn.
Protection from arrest: civil cases only, during a session and 40 days before and after it.
Sita Soren (2024, 7 judges unanimous) overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998, 3:2): no immunity for taking bribes.

Deputy Speaker

Life of the Lok Sabha (normally 5 years)

blocks.title: Removal resolution — key points
items: Removal needs an effective majority, that is, a majority of the House's actual strength (total seats minus vacant seats). Example: 245 seats, 20 vacant, so 225 members; majority is 113.
Notice of 14 days is needed. The notice is given in writing to the Secretary-General of Lok Sabha.
The motion can be taken up only if at least 50 members support it.

While the resolution for his/her removal is being considered (Art 96), the Speaker cannot preside (sit in the chair). He/she can still be present, speak, take part, and vote in the first instance (along with other members) — but cannot give a casting vote (the tie-breaking vote).
The Speaker also loses office if he/she stops being a member of Lok Sabha.
Nabam Rebia case (2016): a Speaker who is facing a notice for his/her own removal should not decide disqualification petitions under the anti-defection law.

blocks.title: Deputy Speaker — special points
items: The Deputy Speaker acts as Speaker when the Speaker's office is vacant or the Speaker is absent, with all the Speaker's powers. When he/she presides, no appeal lies against his/her rulings (decisions cannot be challenged).
Presides over a joint sitting if the Speaker is absent.
The Deputy Speaker is NOT subordinate to (not under) the Speaker; he/she answers directly to the House.
Special privilege: whenever the Deputy Speaker is appointed to any parliamentary committee, he/she automatically becomes its chairman.
When the Speaker is presiding, the Deputy Speaker is like an ordinary member — he/she can speak and vote.
The Constitution does NOT fix a time limit for electing the Deputy Speaker. It also does NOT say the post must go to the opposition.

blocks.text: Origin: the posts of Speaker and Deputy Speaker began in 1921 under the Government of India Act 1919. They were then called President and Deputy President of the Central Legislative Assembly.
The Speaker's powers come from three sources: the Constitution, the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business of Lok Sabha, and parliamentary conventions (accepted practices).

blocks.title: Powers and functions
head: Power
What it means
rows: Keeping order and decorum (discipline) is the main job; the Speaker is the final authority inside the House. Can ask a member to stop and let another speak ('yielding the floor').
Inside the House, the Speaker is the final interpreter of the Constitution, the Rules and past precedents.
If quorum (minimum members needed = 1/10 of total strength) is not present, the Speaker adjourns the House or suspends the sitting until quorum is met.
The Speaker does NOT vote in the first instance (with other members); he/she votes only to break a tie.
Presides over the joint sitting of both Houses (the President summons it)
Decides whether a bill is a money bill, and this decision is final. Signs (endorses) a certificate saying so when the bill goes to Rajya Sabha and to the President.
Decides whether a member is disqualified for defection (changing party). This decision can be challenged in court (judicial review) — Kihoto Hollohan case (1992).
Can allow a secret sitting of the House when the Leader of the House requests it

Appoints the chairmen of all Lok Sabha committees. The Speaker personally chairs the Business Advisory Committee, Rules Committee and General Purposes Committee — NOT the Estimates Committee or the Public Accounts Committee (PAC).
Indian Parliamentary Group (IPG) and presiding officers
Ex officio (automatically) President of the Indian Parliamentary Group; chairs the Conference of Presiding Officers of legislatures in India
Decides whether to admit (accept for discussion) a no-confidence motion, after checking that at least 50 members support it. Admission is not automatic.

When the Speaker 'names' a member for grave disorder, that member is automatically suspended for 5 sittings in a row or for the rest of the session, whichever is shorter. No separate motion of the House is needed.

blocks.title: What the Speaker does NOT have
items: Adjourning the House sine die (ending a sitting without fixing a date to meet again) is a power of the presiding officer. But after prorogation (formal end of the session), only the President can summon the House again (Art 85) — the Speaker cannot.
Does not hold office at the pleasure of the President.
Election is NOT conducted by the Election Commission — the House itself elects.

blocks.title: Independence and impartiality
items: Security of tenure: the Speaker can be removed only by an effective majority (majority of actual members), not by a simple majority (majority of those present and voting).
The Speaker's salary is fixed by Parliament and charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, so it is not voted on every year.
The Speaker's conduct can be discussed in the House only through a substantive motion (a separate, formal motion on that subject).
No court can question the Speaker's rulings on procedure and order in the House.
The Speaker has only a casting vote (tie-breaker), which keeps him/her neutral.
High rank: 7th in the order of precedence, along with the Chief Justice of India.
In Britain, the Speaker gives up party membership on election. In India, this convention has NOT been established.

Courts can examine claims of legislative privilege
Speaker's anti-defection decision is subject to judicial review
In anti-defection cases, the Speaker acts like a tribunal, so courts can review the decision
Expulsion of MPs in the cash-for-query case was valid, but such expulsions can be reviewed by courts
Puts limits on the House's power to expel members

blocks.title: Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha
items: Elected by Rajya Sabha from among its own members (Art 89).
Vacates office if he/she stops being a Rajya Sabha member. Resigns by writing to the Chairman. Can be removed by an effective majority of Rajya Sabha after 14 days' notice (Art 90).
Does the Chairman's duties in three cases: when the Chairman's office is vacant, when the Vice-President is acting as President, or when the Chairman is absent (Art 91).
Not subordinate to (not under) the Chairman; answers directly to the House. Has only a casting vote (tie-breaker) while presiding.
Panel of Vice-Chairpersons: nominated by the Chairman. They cannot preside when the Chairman's or Deputy Chairman's office is vacant — then a member appointed by the President does the job.
Election of the Vice-President (who becomes Chairman): nominated members of both Houses CAN vote, though they cannot vote in the President's election.

blocks.title: Leader of the House vs Leader of Opposition
head: Aspect
Leader of the House
Leader of Opposition (LoP)
rows: An Act of Parliament: Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977 (not the Constitution, not Art 75)
Lok Sabha: the Prime Minister, if he/she is a Lok Sabha member; otherwise a minister nominated by the Prime Minister. Rajya Sabha: a minister nominated by the Prime Minister
Leader of the largest opposition party, recognised by the Speaker (Lok Sabha) or the Chairman (Rajya Sabha)
Gets salary and facilities equal to a Cabinet minister; first recognised in 1969

blocks.title: Leader of Opposition — details
items: First official LoP in Lok Sabha: 1969 (Ram Subhag Singh) — not Morarji Desai.

The 1977 Act itself says only 'leader of the largest opposition party recognised by the presiding officer'. The rule that the party needs one-tenth (1/10) of the seats comes from the Speaker's and Chairman's directions, not from the Act.
So, a party with less than 1/10 of Lok Sabha's strength (55 seats) gets no Leader of Opposition. The figure '75 members' is wrong.
Being recognised as Leader of Opposition and being recognised as a 'party' for facilities under the 1998 Act are two separate tests.
First Lok Sabha: there was no recognised Leader of Opposition. The Swatantra Party (founded 1959) did not even exist then.
1984 elections: Telugu Desam Party (a regional party) became the largest opposition party in Lok Sabha.
In the UK, the opposition forms a 'Shadow Cabinet'. Ivor Jennings called the Leader of Opposition the 'alternative Prime Minister'.

blocks.title: Whips
items: Whips are not in the Constitution, not in the Rules of the House, and not in any statute — they are based only on conventions (accepted practice).
Every party, ruling or opposition, has its own whips.
The government's Chief Whip in Lok Sabha is the Minister of Parliamentary Affairs; in Rajya Sabha it is the Minister of State for Parliamentary Affairs.
The Chief Whip answers to the Leader of the House.

The Leaders and Chief Whips of Recognised Parties and Groups in Parliament (Facilities) Act, 1998 gives phone and staff facilities to the leaders and Chief Whips of recognised parties (at least 55 members in Lok Sabha, at least 25 in Rajya Sabha).

blocks.title: Indian Parliamentary Group (IPG) & forums
items: Indian Parliamentary Group (IPG): an autonomous (self-governing) body formed in 1949, on a motion passed in the Constituent Assembly (Legislative).
Membership: all MPs can be members; former MPs can become associate members.

The Lok Sabha Speaker is its ex officio (automatic) President. The Deputy Speaker and the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman are its ex officio Vice-Presidents. The Lok Sabha Secretary-General is its ex officio Secretary-General.
It works as the National Group of the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU, headquarters in Geneva) AND as the India Branch of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association (CPA).
Purpose: builds contact among MPs, encourages study of public issues, and supports contacts with other parliaments.
Parliamentary forums: help MPs get information on specific issues from experts and officials. The Speaker (not the Deputy Speaker) heads them.

blocks.title: House layout
items: Treasury (government) benches: on the presiding officer's right.
Well: the open area just below the presiding officer's chair and the Table of the House.
Visitors in galleries can never address the House.

blocks.text: Secretariat: each House has its own secretariat. It is headed by a Secretary-General, a permanent officer appointed by the presiding officer.

14th Lok Sabha: Prime Minister Manmohan Singh was a Rajya Sabha member, so Pranab Mukherjee was the Leader of the House in Lok Sabha.
L.K. Advani was the oldest member of the 16th Lok Sabha.

items: The Speaker resigns to the DEPUTY SPEAKER, not to the President.
The President fixes the date of the Speaker's election. The Speaker fixes the date of the Deputy Speaker's election.
When Lok Sabha is dissolved, the Speaker stays in office; the Deputy Speaker goes.
During his/her own removal resolution: the Speaker can vote (in the first instance); the Rajya Sabha Chairman cannot vote at all.
Presiding over a joint sitting and certifying a money bill: done only by the Speaker — never by the Chairman.
The Rajya Sabha Chairman is NOT a member of Rajya Sabha; the Deputy Chairman IS a member.
The Speaker chairs the Business Advisory, Rules and General Purposes Committees — NOT the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) or the Estimates Committee.
Leader of Opposition: a statutory office (1977 Act), first recognised in 1969; the 1/10 seats rule comes from presiding officers' directions. Whip: based only on convention.

subcards.title: Sessions, sittings & devices
subcards.summary: How Parliament meets and ends sittings, and the tools MPs use to question government.
at_a_glance: Art 85 (sessions), Art 100 (voting and quorum), Art 118 (rules of procedure), Art 120 (language), Art 121 (no discussion on judges' conduct), Art 122 (courts cannot question House proceedings)
6 months, counted from the last sitting of one session to the first sitting of the next
1/10 of the total members, including the presiding officer (Lok Sabha 55, Rajya Sabha 25)
The President, on the advice of the Council of Ministers
First hour of the sitting (Lok Sabha: 11 am to 12 noon)
Time right after Question Hour; informal (not in the Rules); an Indian innovation since 1962
Only in Lok Sabha; each needs support of 50 members to be admitted

blocks.title: Key Articles
head: Article
What it says
rows: The President summons each House at such time and place as he thinks fit. The gap between two sessions cannot be more than 6 months. The President prorogues (ends the session of) the Houses and dissolves Lok Sabha.

Art 86: the President may address either House or both together. Art 87: the President must give a special address at the first session after each general election and at the first session of every year.
Questions are decided by a majority of members present and voting. The presiding officer votes only to break a tie (casting vote). Quorum is 1/10 of total members.
Each House makes its own rules of procedure
Business in Parliament is done in Hindi or English
Parliament cannot discuss the conduct of a Supreme Court or High Court judge in their duties, except when a motion to remove that judge is being considered
Courts cannot question the validity of proceedings in Parliament on the ground of irregular procedure

Same two rules for State Legislatures: Art 211 bars a State Legislature from discussing the conduct of any Supreme Court or High Court judge in their duties; Art 212 bars courts from inquiring into State Legislature proceedings

blocks.title: Summoning
items: The President summons (calls) Parliament to meet at any time and place he or she thinks fit.
The maximum gap between two sessions is 6 months, counted from the last sitting of one session to the first sitting of the next. So Parliament must meet at least twice a year.

Usually there are 3 sessions a year: Budget (February to May), Monsoon (July to September) and Winter (November to December). This three-session pattern is only a convention (practice); it is not written in the Constitution.
No minimum number of sitting days per year is fixed by the Constitution.
Why the 6-month rule matters: it keeps the government answerable and ensures regular legislative business.
First session of the first Lok Sabha: 13 May 1952.

blocks.title: Terms that end or pause work
head: Term
Meaning
Done by
Effect on bills
rows: Period from the first sitting of a House until its prorogation (or, for Lok Sabha, its dissolution)
Gap between prorogation and the next session
Pauses a sitting for a fixed time (hours, days or weeks). It ends the sitting, not the session.
Ends a sitting for an indefinite period (sine die means 'without a day': no date is fixed for the next meeting)
Presiding officer (who can also call the House back earlier)
Ends the session (not just the sitting). It usually comes a few days after adjournment sine die, but the President can prorogue a House even while it is in session.
Bills do not lapse (are not cancelled). Pending notices lapse, except notices for introducing bills. (In Britain, by contrast, prorogation ends all pending business.)
Ends the life of Lok Sabha; a new House is formed after elections. Rajya Sabha is a permanent House and is never dissolved.
Most pending business lapses; see the table below

blocks.title: Dissolution of Lok Sabha
items: Lok Sabha is dissolved in two ways: (1) automatically, when its 5-year term (or its extended term during a National Emergency) ends, with no order needed; (2) by the President dissolving it before the term ends.
Early dissolution is done on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Art 74 and Art 85); no Emergency is needed. Once done, it cannot be taken back (irrevocable).
If a government loses a confidence vote and no alternative government can be formed, the President dissolves Lok Sabha and fresh elections follow.
The Council of Ministers does not end when Lok Sabha is dissolved. In U.N.R. Rao v Indira Gandhi (1971), the Supreme Court held that Art 74 requires a Council of Ministers to exist at all times.
The Speaker does not leave office when Lok Sabha is dissolved; he or she continues until just before the first meeting of the new Lok Sabha (see parl-officers).

Lame-duck session: the last session of the old Lok Sabha, held after a new Lok Sabha has been elected. Such sessions were held in 1957 and 1962 to pass the vote on account (advance grant of money for the government). Old members who were not re-elected are called 'lame ducks'.

blocks.title: Lapsing of bills on dissolution of Lok Sabha
head: Bill's position
Lapses?
rows: Pending in Lok Sabha (whether it started in Lok Sabha or was sent by Rajya Sabha)
Passed by Lok Sabha and pending in Rajya Sabha
Pending in Rajya Sabha and not yet passed by Lok Sabha
The two Houses disagreed, and the President had notified a joint sitting before the dissolution
Passed by both Houses and waiting for the President's assent
Passed by both Houses and returned by the President for reconsideration
blocks.note: Memory rule: a bill lapses only if it is 'in the hands' of the outgoing Lok Sabha, that is, pending in Lok Sabha, or passed by Lok Sabha and waiting in Rajya Sabha. Motions, resolutions, notices and petitions pending before Lok Sabha or its committees also lapse. Assurances pending before the Committee on Government Assurances do not lapse. Example: the first Lokpal Bill (1968) was passed by Lok Sabha but lapsed when Lok Sabha was dissolved.

blocks.text: See Legislative procedure (joint sitting and President's assent)

blocks.title: Quorum (Art 100)
items: Quorum is the minimum number of members who must be present for the House to do business: 1/10 of the total members of the House, including the presiding officer.
So the quorum is 55 in Lok Sabha and 25 in Rajya Sabha.
Quorum is laid down in Art 100, not Art 118 (Art 118 only lets each House make its own rules).
If there is no quorum, the presiding officer must adjourn the House or suspend the meeting until enough members are present.
For a joint sitting of both Houses, the quorum is 1/10 of the total members of the two Houses together.

blocks.title: Voting
items: Matters are decided by a simple majority of members present and voting (not counting the presiding officer). A special or effective majority is needed only where the Constitution says so.
The presiding officer does not vote at first; he or she uses a casting vote only when there is a tie.
Proceedings remain valid even if some seats are vacant or someone not entitled took part.

Voting methods in Lok Sabha: (1) voice vote, where members say 'Ayes' or 'Noes'; (2) division, a recorded vote using the automatic vote recorder, 'Aye' and 'No' slips, or members going into the lobbies (the lobby method is now obsolete); (3) secret ballot, where the member's display light flashes only white so the vote is not shown; (4) physical count, where members are counted but names are not recorded; (5) casting vote of the presiding officer.
Division process: if the Speaker's decision on a voice vote is challenged, the Speaker orders the lobby to be cleared and puts the question again after 3 minutes 30 seconds.

blocks.title: Language (Art 120) and right to speak
items: Business is done in Hindi or English; the presiding officer may allow a member to speak in his or her mother tongue.
Simultaneous interpretation (live translation) is available for the languages in the Eighth Schedule.
English was to stop being used in the House after 15 years (that is, in 1965), but the Official Languages Act 1963 allowed it to continue.

Ministers and the Attorney General can speak in either House, in a joint sitting and in committees, but they can vote only in the House of which they are members. A person can be a minister for up to 6 months without being a member of Parliament.
So a Prime Minister who is a Rajya Sabha member can speak in Lok Sabha but cannot vote there, for example on a no-confidence motion.

blocks.title: Question Hour – types of questions
head: Type
Answer
Supplementaries?
Notes
rows: Allowed only if it relates to a bill, resolution or other matter that member is in charge of; list printed yellow
blocks.note: Question Hour is the first hour of every sitting (Lok Sabha: 11 am to 12 noon). The list of short-notice questions is printed light pink. Rajya Sabha moved its Question Hour to 12 noon to 1 pm in 2014.

blocks.title: Discussion devices
head: Device
What / when
Formal motion & vote?
rows: The time from the end of Question Hour until the regular agenda starts. MPs raise urgent matters without prior notice. It is NOT in the Rules of Procedure, so it is informal. An Indian innovation since 1962.
For a matter of enough public importance that has been debated a lot, where the answer needs clarifying on facts. The Speaker can allot 3 days a week.
Short duration discussion (also called two-hour discussion; Lok Sabha Rule 193)
For an urgent public matter; time limit 2 hours; the Speaker can allot 2 days a week; in use since 1953. The notice must be supported by at least 2 other members (not 50).
Special Mention (Rajya Sabha) and Notice under Rule 377 (Lok Sabha)
For a matter that cannot be raised through any other device
Raised when the proceedings break the Rules of Procedure or the Articles on procedure. It is an extraordinary device that suspends the proceedings, and is usually used by the Opposition.

blocks.text: There is no device called 'full-day discussion'. Zero Hour is not a formally prescribed device; it is only a convention (practice).
No discussion on a matter of general public importance can take place except on a motion moved with the presiding officer's consent.

Most resolutions are not legally binding on the government. The mover cannot withdraw a resolution without the leave (permission) of the House.

blocks.title: Youth Parliament
items: Started on the recommendation of the Fourth All India Whips Conference.
Aim: teach youth parliamentary procedure, discipline, tolerance and democratic values.
The Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs (not the Election Commission) gives training and encouragement to states for Youth Parliament.

blocks.title: House conduct and terms
items: Treasury benches (seats of the government side): on the presiding officer's right; the Opposition sits on the left.

Well of the House: the low open area just in front of the presiding officer's chair, where the Table of the House is (it is not the visitors' gallery). Visitors in the galleries can never address the House.
Yielding the floor: when the Speaker asks a member to stop speaking so that another member can speak.

Lok Sabha Rule 373: the Speaker can order a disorderly member to leave the House for the rest of the day. Rule 374: the Speaker names the member, and the House (by a motion) can suspend him or her for up to the rest of the session. Rule 374A (grave disorder): once the Speaker names the member, the member is automatically suspended for 5 consecutive sittings or the rest of the session, whichever is less; no separate motion is needed.
Rajya Sabha Rule 255: the Chairman can order a member to withdraw from the House. Rule 256: suspension of a member needs a motion passed by the House.

Unparliamentary words (words not allowed in the House): a 2022 Lok Sabha Secretariat booklet listed words like 'shakuni', 'nautanki', 'girgit' and 'jumlajeevi'. 'Chakkar' is not in the reported list (asked in an exam). If a member uses such a word, the presiding officer expunges it (removes it from the official record).

The Speaker or Chairman adjourns the House (including adjournment sine die); only the President summons and prorogues. The presiding officer's power to adjourn sine die comes from the Rules of Procedure, not from the Constitution.
Prorogation ends a session, not the House, and bills do not lapse. Dissolution ends the Lok Sabha itself.
The 6-month gap is counted from the last sitting of one session to the first sitting of the next. Three sessions a year is only a convention.
Quorum 1/10 is in Art 100, not Art 118.
No-confidence motion: Lok Sabha only, 50 members, no reasons needed, against the whole ministry. Censure motion: reasons needed, and it can target even one minister.
Adjournment motion: needs 50 members, not used in Rajya Sabha, carries an element of censure, and cannot be on a sub judice matter (one pending in court).
Zero Hour (since 1962) is not in the Rules; Calling attention motion (since 1954) is in the Rules; both are Indian innovations.
Starred question: oral answer, supplementary questions allowed. Unstarred question: written answer, no supplementary questions, no asterisk mark. Discussion under Rule 193: no voting.

Dissolution of the House is not a tool of legislative control over the administration (it is the President's power). Tools of control are questions, Zero Hour, motions (adjournment, no-confidence, censure), resolutions and committees.

sections.heading: Bills: kinds and who brings them

blocks.text: A bill is a proposal for a law. All legislative proposals come to Parliament as bills. A bill becomes an Act only after both Houses pass it and the President gives assent.

blocks.title: Private members' bills — extra facts
items: Lok Sabha has a Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions. It has 15 members, is chaired by the Deputy Speaker, and its term is up to 1 year. It sorts these bills into categories and suggests how much time to give for discussing each.
This committee exists only in Lok Sabha. Private members CAN still introduce bills in Rajya Sabha.
Only 14 private members' bills have ever become law, and the last one was in 1970. So the exam statement 'a private member's bill was recently passed for the first time ever' is false.

In 2015 Rajya Sabha passed Tiruchi Siva's Rights of Transgender Persons Bill. It was the first private member's bill passed by Rajya Sabha in about 45 years. It did not become law (Lok Sabha did not pass it).

children.label: Ordinary bill: any matter other than financial matters
Money bill: contains only Art 110 matters; follows the special procedure of Art 109
Financial bill (I) under Art 117(1), and Financial bill (II) under Art 117(3)

blocks.title: By content (Laxmikanth)
items: Original bills (new law), amending bills (change an existing law), consolidating bills (combine several laws into one), expiring laws (continuance) bills (extend a law that would expire), repealing bills (cancel a law), validating bills (make past actions legal)
Bills to replace ordinances, Constitution amendment bills, and money and financial bills

blocks.title: Ordinary bill: from idea to Act

steps.detail: The bill can be introduced in EITHER House, by a minister or a private member, after taking permission ('leave') of the House. The mover reads only its title and objectives; there is no discussion. The bill is then published in the Gazette. (If it was already published in the Gazette before introduction, leave of the House is not needed.)

(a) General discussion: the House discusses the main principles of the bill. The House may then take it up at once, send it to a Select Committee (members of one House only), send it to a Joint Committee (members of both Houses), or circulate it to get public opinion. (b) Committee stage: the committee studies the bill clause by clause. It can amend the clauses but cannot change the main principle. (c) Consideration stage: the House votes on each clause; amendments can be moved.

The House only accepts or rejects the bill as a whole; no amendments are allowed. It is passed by a majority of members present and voting. The presiding officer then signs (authenticates) it and sends it to the other House.

The bill goes through the same three readings. The second House can pass it as it is, pass it with amendments and send it back, reject it, or not act on it at all. Rajya Sabha can hold an ordinary bill for up to 6 months.
A deadlock arises if the other House rejects the bill, if the Houses finally disagree on amendments, or if 6 months pass with no action. Then the President may call a joint sitting (Art 108).
The President may give assent, withhold assent, or return the bill once for reconsideration. See the card 'President: veto, ordinance, pardon'.

blocks.text: See 'President: veto, ordinance, pardon' for assent, the kinds of veto and pocket veto
Both Houses have EQUAL power over an ordinary bill. For what happens to pending bills on prorogation (end of a session) or dissolution of Lok Sabha, see the card 'Sessions, sittings & devices'.
See 'Sessions, sittings & devices' for lapsing of bills

blocks.title: Art 110: a bill is a money bill if it has ONLY these matters
head: Matter
rows: Imposing, abolishing, remitting, altering or regulating any tax
Regulating borrowing by the Union, or giving of guarantees by the Government of India
Custody of the Consolidated Fund or Contingency Fund of India, and paying money into or taking money out of these funds
Appropriation of money out of the Consolidated Fund of India
Declaring any expenditure 'charged' on the Consolidated Fund, or increasing it
Receipt of money into the Consolidated Fund or the Public Account of India, and audit of the accounts of the Union or of a state
blocks.note: A bill is NOT a money bill just because it provides for fines or penalties, fees for licences or services, or taxes by a local body for local purposes.

blocks.title: Who decides
items: Art 110(3): if doubt arises, the Speaker of Lok Sabha decides; the decision is final.
It cannot be questioned in any court, in either House, or by the President (Laxmikanth).
Speaker endorses a certificate on it when sending to Rajya Sabha and to the President.
If the Speaker's office is vacant, the Deputy Speaker performs the Speaker's duties (Art 95), including this one.
The Rajya Sabha Chairman, the Finance Minister, the Prime Minister and the President do NOT certify a money bill.

steps.detail: It can be introduced only by a minister (so it is always a government bill) and only on the President's recommendation.
Speaker certifies it as a money bill.
Rajya Sabha cannot reject or amend it. It can only make recommendations and must return it within 14 days.

Lok Sabha may accept or reject any or all recommendations. Either way the bill is deemed passed by both Houses. If Rajya Sabha does not return it in 14 days, it is deemed passed as Lok Sabha passed it.
Assents or withholds assent; CANNOT return it for reconsideration. Normally assents, as it came with his prior recommendation.

blocks.title: Why no joint sitting on a money bill
items: Lok Sabha has overriding power and Rajya Sabha can only recommend, so no deadlock can arise.
Same rule in states with a Legislative Council: the Council can only recommend within 14 days.

head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters

blocks.text: Every money bill is a financial bill, but every financial bill is not a money bill. A money bill has ONLY Art 110 matters; a financial bill mixes them with other matters, or merely involves spending.

head: Aspect
Financial bill (I) — Art 117(1)
Financial bill (II) — Art 117(3)

Spending from the Consolidated Fund, but no Art 110 matter
Not needed for introduction; needed before the House takes it up for CONSIDERATION (discussion and passing)
Can amend or reject it (an amendment, other than one reducing or abolishing a tax, needs the President's recommendation)

head: Feature
Ordinary bill
Money bill (Art 110)
Financial bill (I and II, Art 117)
Constitution Amendment bill (Art 368)

Full power: can amend, reject or hold it for 6 months
Can only recommend; must return it in 14 days
Full power: can amend or reject

See 'Budget and financial control' for the Appropriation Bill, the Finance Bill and demands for grants

steps.detail: Other House rejects the bill; OR Houses finally disagree on amendments; OR more than 6 months pass without the other House passing it (days when that House is prorogued or adjourned for more than 4 consecutive days are not counted).

The President 'may' summon it (it is not compulsory) and acts on the advice of the ministers. The Constitution does not say the bill lapses if no joint sitting is called; it stays pending (it can still lapse later, for example on dissolution of Lok Sabha).

After the President notifies intention, neither House can proceed with the bill. If Lok Sabha is dissolved after this notice, the bill does NOT lapse. If the bill already lapsed by dissolution, no joint sitting is possible.

The Speaker presides. If absent, the Deputy Speaker; if also absent, the Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha; if also absent, a person chosen by the members present. The Chairman of Rajya Sabha never presides, because he is not a member of either House. Quorum (minimum members needed) is one-tenth of the total members of both Houses. The Rules of Procedure of Lok Sabha apply.
No new amendments can be proposed except (a) those that caused the final disagreement, or (b) those that became necessary because of delay in passing the bill.
Passed by a majority of the total members of both Houses PRESENT AND VOTING (simple majority). Lok Sabha usually wins because it has more members.

Not available: money bills (Lok Sabha overrides) and Constitution Amendment bills (each House must pass separately)

items: If the needed recommendation or sanction was not obtained beforehand, the Act is still valid if the President (or Governor) later gives assent.
So courts cannot strike down a law only because prior sanction was missing.
A prior recommendation does NOT take away the President's power to return an ordinary (e.g. Art 3) bill.
A private member is any MP who is not a minister; being nominated has nothing to do with it.
Money bill: introduced only in Lok Sabha, only by a minister, only with the President's recommendation. Rajya Sabha gets 14 days and can only recommend.
The Speaker certifies a money bill (not the President, Finance Minister or Rajya Sabha Chairman), and the decision is final.
All money bills are financial bills; not all financial bills are money bills.

subcards.title: Budget & financial control
subcards.summary: How Parliament passes the budget and controls every rupee the government spends.
at_a_glance: Called the 'Annual Financial Statement' (Art 112); the word 'budget' is not used in the Constitution
Art 112 to Art 117 (budget procedure), Art 265 (tax only by law), Art 266 and Art 267 (the funds)
1 February (since 2017); earlier it was the last working day of February
Separated from the General Budget in 1924 (on the Acworth Committee report of 1921); merged back in 2017
Who votes the demands for grants
Lok Sabha only (Art 113); Rajya Sabha can only discuss
Budget Division of the Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance
Art 267; created by the Contingency Fund of India Act, 1950; corpus ₹30,000 crore (raised from ₹500 crore by the Finance Act, 2021)

blocks.text: The budget is a statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India for one financial year (1 April to 31 March). The Constitution calls it the 'Annual Financial Statement' (Art 112); the word 'budget' appears nowhere in it.

blocks.title: What the budget contains
items: Estimates of revenue and capital receipts
Ways and means to raise the revenue (how the money will be collected)
Estimates of expenditure
Actual receipts and expenditure of the closing year, with reasons for any deficit or surplus
Economic and financial policy for the coming year (tax proposals, spending programme, new schemes)

blocks.title: Constitutional provisions on the budget
head: Article
Rule
rows: The President causes the Annual Financial Statement to be laid before BOTH Houses. It shows 'charged' expenditure (not voted) and other expenditure (voted) separately, and also separates expenditure on revenue account from other expenditure.

No demand for grant can be made except on the President's recommendation. Only the Lok Sabha votes on demands. The Lok Sabha can approve, refuse or reduce a demand, but can never increase it. Charged expenditure is not put to vote, but it can be discussed.

No money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund except under an appropriation made by law (the Appropriation Act). No amendment can be moved to the Appropriation Bill that changes the amount or the purpose (destination) of a grant, or changes the amount of any charged expenditure.
Allows the vote on account (advance grant for part of the year), the vote of credit (for an unexpected need whose details cannot be given) and exceptional grants.

Financial bills: a bill that imposes a tax needs the President's recommendation and cannot be introduced in the Rajya Sabha. No recommendation is needed for an amendment that reduces or abolishes a tax. So Parliament can reduce or abolish a tax, but cannot increase it.

Money bill procedure: introduced only in the Lok Sabha. The Rajya Sabha must return it within 14 days, with or without recommendations, and the Lok Sabha may accept or reject those recommendations. The budget's Finance Bill and Appropriation Bill are passed as money bills.
No tax can be levied (imposed) or collected except by authority of law.

blocks.title: Who does what
head: Body
Role
rows: Causes the budget to be laid (Art 112); recommends demands for grants and money bills; the Contingency Fund is at the President's disposal; constitutes the Finance Commission
Presents the budget in the Lok Sabha with the 'budget speech'. The budget is laid on behalf of the President, not the Prime Minister.
Department of Economic Affairs (Budget Division), Ministry of Finance
Prepares the budget and presents it to Parliament through the Finance Minister
Administrative ministries and the CAG (Comptroller and Auditor General)
Help in preparing the estimates and accounts
NOT involved in preparing the budget. It only recommends how taxes are shared between the Union and the States (see the Finance Commission card).

blocks.title: Rajya Sabha's limited role
head: Aspect
Lok Sabha
Rajya Sabha
rows: Yes, it can discuss the budget
Money bill or Finance Bill on tax
Cannot reject or amend it; can only make recommendations within 14 days
Considering CAG reports; approving an Emergency proclamation

blocks.text: Railway budget: it was separated from the General Budget in 1924 on the report of the Acworth Committee (1921). The aims were flexibility in railway finance, a business approach to railway policy, and a fixed yearly contribution from railways to general revenues. It was merged into the Union Budget in 2017. Even when it was separate, railway spending was under the same parliamentary control as all other spending.
See Legislative procedure: money bills (Art 110) and financial bills (Art 117)

sections.heading: Six stages of the budget in Parliament

steps.detail: The Finance Minister presents the budget in the Lok Sabha on 1 February with the budget speech; it is then laid in the Rajya Sabha. There is no discussion on the day it is presented. The budget can also be presented in two or more parts.
Both Houses discuss the budget as a whole for 3 to 4 days. No cut motion can be moved and nothing is voted at this stage. The Finance Minister replies at the end.
The Houses adjourn for 3 to 4 weeks. The 24 Departmentally Related Standing Committees (DRSCs) examine the demands for grants of their ministries and report to both Houses.

Only in the Lok Sabha. Demands are taken ministry by ministry, and each demand is voted separately. Cut motions are moved at this stage. Once voted, a demand becomes a 'grant'. On the last day the guillotine is applied (all remaining demands are voted at once).

Allows money to be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund for the voted grants and for the charged expenditure. No amendment can change the amount or purpose of a grant. Once passed, it becomes the Appropriation Act.

Puts the tax proposals (the income side of the budget) into effect. It is passed as a money bill, but amendments to reject or reduce a tax ARE allowed. It must be enacted within 75 days, because tax changes collected provisionally under the Provisional Collection of Taxes Act (the 1931 Act, replaced by the Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, 2023) lapse after 75 days.

blocks.text: Memory line: Presentation, General discussion, Committee scrutiny, Voting on demands, Appropriation Bill, Finance Bill. The vote on account is passed right after the general discussion.

head: Aspect
Appropriation Bill
Finance Bill

Amendments to reject or reduce a tax can be moved
Passed as a money bill (money bill rules apply)

blocks.title: Documents presented with the budget (Laxmikanth list)

Note
rows: Budget Speech; Annual Financial Statement; Demands for Grants; Finance Bill
Macro-Economic Framework Statement; Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement; Medium Term Fiscal Policy Statement
Required by the FRBM Act, 2003 (Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act), not by the Constitution

Expenditure Budget; Receipts Budget; Expenditure Profile; Memorandum on Finance Bill; Budget at a Glance; Outcome Budget; Key Features; Implementation of Previous Announcements; Key to Budget Documents

blocks.title: Departmentally Related Standing Committees in budget scrutiny
items: Set up in 1993 on the recommendation of the Rules Committee of the Lok Sabha (17 committees at first, expanded to 24 in 2004)

They examine the demands for grants before the Lok Sabha votes on them. They also examine bills referred to them, annual reports of ministries, and national basic long-term policy documents referred by the Speaker or the Rajya Sabha Chairman.
Purpose: closer and more detailed financial control over ministries. Their reports only advise; they do not replace the decision of the House.

Charged on Consolidated Fund
Made from Consolidated Fund (voted)

head: Item
rows: Emoluments, allowances and office expenses of the President
Salaries and allowances of the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, and of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha
Salaries, allowances and pensions of Supreme Court judges

Any sum needed to pay a judgement, decree or award of any court or arbitral tribunal
Any other expenditure that Parliament by law declares to be charged
blocks.note: NOT charged: the salaries of the Prime Minister and other ministers (these are voted). Salaries of State Public Service Commission members are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the STATE, not of India.

blocks.text: States (Art 202 and Art 203) follow the same scheme. Charged expenditure of a State (for example, High Court judges' salaries and the Governor's emoluments) is not put to the vote of the Legislative Assembly, but it CAN be discussed (Art 203(1)).

blocks.title: Three kinds of cut motion

Wording
Purpose

'The demand be reduced BY a specified amount'
Shows the saving (economy) that can be made: either a lump-sum cut or removing or reducing a particular item
Raises (ventilates) a specific grievance that falls within the responsibility of the Government of India

blocks.title: Conditions for a cut motion to be admissible
items: It must relate to only ONE demand
It must be clearly worded, without arguments or defamatory (insulting) statements
Confined to one specific matter
It must not suggest amending or repealing existing laws
It must relate to a matter that is mainly the Union's concern
It must not relate to charged expenditure

It must not raise a question of privilege

items: It focuses the debate on one specific demand
It upholds responsible government, because members can question the executive's work
In practice it is rarely passed, as the government has a majority. If one is passed, it shows the government lacks the confidence of the Lok Sabha, and the government may have to resign.
If the budget or a finance measure is defeated in the Lok Sabha, the Prime Minister submits the resignation of the whole Council of Ministers

blocks.text: Guillotine: on the last day allotted for voting, the Speaker puts all the remaining demands to vote at once, whether they have been discussed or not.

Vote on account (Art 116)
Interim budget

After the general discussion on the budget

blocks.text: Rule of lapse: voted money that is not spent by the end of the financial year (31 March) lapses (cannot be carried forward). This causes a 'rush of expenditure' (the March rush) near the year-end. The Appropriation Act also comes to an end once its purpose for that year is served.

subcards.title: Parliamentary Committees
subcards.summary: Committees are small groups of MPs who do Parliament's detailed checking work and report back to the House.
at_a_glance: They come from the Rules of each House; the Constitution only mentions them (Art 105, Art 118)
Standing committees (permanent) and ad hoc committees (temporary — they end when their task is done)

Public Accounts Committee (PAC): 22 members (15 Lok Sabha and 7 Rajya Sabha). Estimates Committee: 30 members, all from Lok Sabha. Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU): 22 members (15 Lok Sabha and 7 Rajya Sabha)

Appointed by the Lok Sabha Speaker; since 1967 the chairman has been an Opposition member — this is a convention (practice), not a written rule
Most committees serve for 1 year; ministers cannot be members
Committee reports are only advice — they never bind the government
K.C. Venugopal (Congress) is PAC chairman, reappointed for 2026–27 (as of Nov 2026)

blocks.text: Parliament is too big and too busy to study every bill or account in detail. So it hands the detailed work to small groups of MPs called committees. They study, then report back; Parliament decides.

blocks.title: A 'parliamentary committee' must satisfy all 4 conditions
items: It is appointed or elected by the House, or nominated by the Speaker (Lok Sabha) or the Chairman (Rajya Sabha)
It works under the direction of the Speaker or the Chairman
It reports to the House or to the Speaker or the Chairman
Its office staff (secretariat) is provided by the Lok Sabha Secretariat or the Rajya Sabha Secretariat
Consultative Committees do not meet these conditions, so they are NOT parliamentary committees (see the section 'Not parliamentary committees')

Each House makes its own Rules of Procedure. The size, term and work of committees come from these rules
Ministers and the Attorney-General may speak and take part in a committee in which they are named as members, but Art 88 does not give them a vote
The Constitution does NOT specifically set up the PAC, the DRSCs or any other committee; it only mentions committees
